title: Scrutiny of the 2026 KIIFB Expert Review Committee
description: Comprehensive institutional, legal, and biographical scrutiny of the Expert Committee constituted under G.O.(P) No.80/2026/FIN dated 13.07.2026, documenting procedural lapses, member records, and positional conflicts of interest.

legal_constitution.statutory_inquiry_status: Non-Statutory (Not constituted under the Commissions of Inquiry Act, 1952)
legal_constitution.jurisdictional_paradox: The Committee was constituted by an executive order of the Finance Department to review, evaluate, and identify 'deviations' in a statutory corporation established by a plenary Act of the Kerala State Legislature (Act 4 of 2000 as amended by Act 8 of 2016). An administrative panel convened by executive fiat has no constitutional standing to invalidate, alter, or pronounce void the legislative mandates established by the sovereign State Assembly.
legal_constitution.mandate_summary: To undertake a comprehensive review of the institutional, financial, governance, and operational framework of KIIFB, covering 11 specific Terms of Reference (ToR).

procedural_and_positional_lapses.title: Pre-Determined & Asymmetric Terms of Reference (ToR 1 & 2)
procedural_and_positional_lapses.official_record: Chapter I (para 1.1) & Chapter II of Committee Report
procedural_and_positional_lapses.description: Terms of Reference 1 and 2 explicitly mandated the Committee to judge KIIFB's functioning against the 2014 Concept Note prepared by SBI Capital Markets Ltd and the Chandrasekhar Committee under the previous UDF administration. This framed an unlegislated, executive merchant-banking advisory concept note as the sacrosanct normative standard, while treating the subsequent statutory enactment passed by the Kerala Legislative Assembly (Act 8 of 2016) as an aberrant 'deviation'.
procedural_and_positional_lapses.implication: Pre-judged the outcome of the inquiry by treating the expansion of infrastructure to social sectors (schools, hospitals) and statutory revenue hypothecation as unauthorized deviations rather than sovereign legislative choices made by an elected parliament.

procedural_and_positional_lapses.title: Constitutional Sub Judice Intrusion
procedural_and_positional_lapses.official_record: Supreme Court Original Suit No. 1 of 2024 & Kerala High Court WP(C) 27076/2022
procedural_and_positional_lapses.description: The Committee rendered extensive administrative findings on whether KIIFB borrowings violate Article 293(3) and whether Masala Bonds infringe Entry 37 of List I, despite knowing that both matters were actively sub judice before constitutional courts. On 1 April 2024, the Supreme Court of India referred the question of Union borrowing deductions under Article 293 to a 5-Judge Constitution Bench in State of Kerala v. Union of India. Similarly, the Kerala High Court granted stay orders in the Masala Bond FEMA inquiry.
procedural_and_positional_lapses.implication: An executive panel purported to pass judgment on questions that the highest court of the land has formally determined to be undecided constitutional controversies pending Constitution Bench adjudication.

procedural_and_positional_lapses.title: Structural Conflicts of Interest in Panel Appointments
procedural_and_positional_lapses.description: The Government appointed individuals with direct structural conflicts of interest. Tarun Bajaj, former Union Revenue and Economic Affairs Secretary (2020–2022), was at the helm of the Union Ministry of Finance when the Department of Expenditure enacted the policy deducting State SPV debt from Net Borrowing Ceilings (costing Kerala ₹25,932.55 Cr). Shyam Srinivasan was MD & CEO of Federal Bank, which held a 5.61% equity stake in KIIFB's asset management affiliate Kerala Infrastructure Fund Management Limited (KIFML, Table 5.6).
procedural_and_positional_lapses.implication: Violated the fundamental natural justice maxim 'nemo judex in causa sua' (no one should be a judge in their own cause). The panel included both an architect of the Union's borrowing clampdown and a representative of a banking institution with equity exposure in KIIFB's corporate structure.

procedural_and_positional_lapses.title: Bypassing Legislative Tabling & Oversight Protocols
procedural_and_positional_lapses.official_record: Letter of Transmittal dated 13 October 2026 to Additional Chief Secretary (Finance)
procedural_and_positional_lapses.description: The Committee submitted its report directly to the Additional Chief Secretary (Finance) on 13 October 2026. The findings were disseminated and deployed administratively before being tabled on the floor of the Kerala Legislative Assembly or referred to the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) or the Committee on Public Undertakings (COPU).
procedural_and_positional_lapses.implication: Circumvented legislative scrutiny over a statutory corporation created by the Assembly, using an internal executive document as a public verdict without providing the statutory Board an institutional right of reply on the floor of the House.

members.name: Sudha Pillai
members.career_background: Former Member Secretary, Planning Commission of India (2009–2014); Secretary, Union Ministry of Labour & Employment; Union Joint Secretary (Industry); Principal Secretary, Finance and Industries, Government of Kerala; District Collector, Thiruvananthapuram.
members.primary_expertise: Central economic planning, labour administration, public enterprise governance, and central bureaucracy.
members.positional_bias: Deeply embedded in the centralist technocratic culture of the erstwhile Union Planning Commission. Tends toward conventional public finance orthodoxy where capital investment must conform to central macro-ceilings, with deep skepticism toward sub-national autonomous financing mechanisms outside traditional departmental hierarchies.
members.documented_conflict: None direct commercial, but structural ideological alignment with Central Union planning over sub-national fiscal innovation.

members.name: Tarun Bajaj
members.career_background: Former Union Revenue Secretary (2021–2022); Secretary, Department of Economic Affairs (DEA, 2020–2021), Ministry of Finance, Government of India; Additional Secretary, Prime Minister's Office (PMO, 2015–2020); Joint Secretary, Department of Financial Services (DFS).
members.primary_expertise: Union fiscal management, central tax policy, financial sector regulation, and macro-economic borrowing limits.
members.positional_bias: Architect of Union fiscal centralism. Staunch defender of the Union Ministry of Finance's prerogative to enforce rigid Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) ceilings on states. Spearheaded the Central Government's tightening of off-budget borrowing norms.
members.documented_conflict: EXTREME CONFLICT OF INTEREST: Tarun Bajaj was the executive head of the Union Ministry of Finance during 2021–2022 when the Department of Expenditure formulated and issued the landmark guidelines treating borrowings by State SPVs/corporations as State Government debt under Article 293(3). This very policy resulted in the ₹25,932.55 Crore deduction from Kerala's Net Borrowing Ceiling between 2022-23 and 2026-27 (Table 3.11 of the Committee's report). Appointing the very central official who designed and executed the financial squeeze on Kerala to sit as an impartial arbiter on KIIFB's borrowing structure is a flagrant institutional conflict of interest.

members.name: Shyam Srinivasan
members.service_cadre: Private Commercial Banking (Former MD & CEO, The Federal Bank Ltd)
members.career_background: Managing Director & CEO of The Federal Bank Ltd for 14 years (2010–2024); extensive senior leadership roles at Standard Chartered Bank, Citibank, and across Asian emerging markets; Chairman of CII Kerala State Council.
members.primary_expertise: Commercial banking, retail lending, corporate credit appraisal, NPA recovery, and private capital asset quality.
members.positional_bias: Commercial banking profitability paradigm. Evaluates infrastructure financing through the prism of debt servicing coverage ratios (DSCR), direct escrow cash flows, and collateral liquidability. Inherently averse to financing non-monetizable social public goods (schools, hospitals) using debt.
members.documented_conflict: COMMERCIAL & EQUITY CONFLICT OF INTEREST: Federal Bank, under Shyam Srinivasan's leadership, was an equity partner holding 5.61% of Kerala Infrastructure Fund Management Limited (KIFML), KIIFB's asset management affiliate (Table 5.6 of the Committee report). Furthermore, Federal Bank acted as a major commercial banker and depository in Kerala. A former chief executive of an equity partner in a KIIFB affiliate sat on a panel evaluating the institutional structure, financial viability, and restructuring of those very entities.

members.name: Nilesh Vikamsey
members.career_background: Senior Partner at Khimji Kunverji & Co LLP; President of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI, 2017–2018); Chairman of SEBI's Qualified Audit Report Review Committee; Board Member of the International Federation of Accountants (IFAC); Independent Director on corporate boards.
members.primary_expertise: Corporate statutory audit, Indian Accounting Standards (IndAS / IFRS), forensic accounting, and corporate balance sheet consolidation.
members.positional_bias: Corporate accounting orthodoxy. Judges sovereign capital formation using corporate accounting standards (GAAP/IndAS), demanding matching commercial revenue streams for liabilities. Views statutory escrowing of state revenues as off-balance-sheet opacity rather than sovereign credit enhancement for public goods.
members.documented_conflict: Applies private corporate insolvency and cash-flow accounting metrics to sovereign state developmental spending, where public benefits accrue as socio-economic externalities rather than balance sheet receipts.

members.name: H. Shubhalakshmi Narayanan
members.career_background: Senior corporate governance, audit, and financial compliance expert; advisor on regulatory structures and internal risk management systems.
members.primary_expertise: Internal financial controls, regulatory compliance, risk management frameworks, and organizational process auditing.
members.positional_bias: Technocratic compliance focus. Prioritizes procedural conformity with traditional Secretariat financial rules over sub-national developmental speed and agile execution.
members.documented_conflict: Institutional conservatism: treating administrative departures from traditional departmental procedures as inherent financial irregularities.

key_advisors.name: K.M. Chandrasekhar
key_advisors.background: Former Cabinet Secretary to the Government of India (2007–2011); former Vice Chairman of the Kerala State Planning Board (2011–2016 under the UDF administration); author of the 2014 Chandrasekhar Committee Report on KIIFB restructuring with SBI Caps.
key_advisors.notable_context: The Committee's Foreword acknowledges the 'guidance and support received from Mr. K.M. Chandrasekhar'. K.M. Chandrasekhar was the very architect of the 2014 SBI Caps restructuring plan that Terms of Reference 1 & 2 set up as the ideal model from which the 2016 LDF model was accused of 'deviating'. Thus, the author of the 2014 proposal actively guided the panel evaluating the 2016 legislature's decision to supersede his model.

key_advisors.name: Prof. D. Narayana
key_advisors.role: Economic Advisor to the Vice Chairperson
key_advisors.background: Former Director of the Centre for Development Studies (CDS); Chief Economic Advisor to the Vice Chairperson, Kerala State Planning Board.
key_advisors.contribution: Assisted the Committee in interpreting macro-fiscal trajectories and debt sustainability.

key_advisors.name: Prof. M. Parameswaran
key_advisors.background: Associate Professor, Centre for Development Studies (CDS).
key_advisors.contribution: Facilitated panel discussions, statistical computations, and drafting of chapters.

political_and_fiscal_timing.context: Constituted in July 2026 and submitted in October 2026. The timing coincides with the culmination of four convergent pressures on the State of Kerala:
factors: The cumulative Union Ministry of Finance deductions under Article 293(3) reached ₹25,932.55 Crore (2022-23 to 2026-27), suffocating the State Treasury's day-to-day liquidity.
The start of the 16-year debt service amortisation cliff (Table 6.1) requiring ₹47,532.54 Crore in principal and interest repayments up to 2041-42.
An estimated ₹22,883.00 Crore required over five years (2026-27 to 2030-31) to complete ongoing physical infrastructure projects (Table 6.3).

Preparation for upcoming state legislative budget cycles, providing the executive with a technocratic justification to take over KIIFB's liabilities, cancel Section 7 revenue hypothecation, and halt further autonomous borrowing.

nature_of_the_report.epistemic_character: The report presents itself as an objective financial and institutional review, but operates under a specific ideological doctrine: orthodox fiscal conservatism. It treats a sovereign Legislative Assembly Act as a series of 'deviations' from an unlegislated merchant bank note, views social infrastructure (schools and hospitals) as a fiscal drag because they lack user fees, and aligns seamlessly with the Union Government's efforts to restrict sub-national borrowing autonomy.
